title: Fracture / Splinting Guide

changelog.change: Deepened to a 2-level tree — per region a displacement/pattern triage (splint as-is vs reduce vs emergent ortho), key named fractures (scaphoid, boxer's, Jones, Lisfranc, supracondylar), a shared compartment-syndrome and emergent-ortho node, and a pediatric-pattern branch (buckle / Salter-Harris / plastic deformation).
Initial entry — region → splint type / position / neurovascular check / red flags.

purpose: Region → pattern triage → splint type + position + the neurovascular check that matters, or a reduction / emergent-ortho branch. Includes the common named fractures and paediatric patterns.
entryPrompt: Which region — or is this a paediatric growth-plate pattern?

choices.label: ⚠ Screen for an emergent pattern first

nodes.prompt: First — any of: open fracture, hard sign of vascular injury (absent pulse, expanding haematoma, bruit), progressive neuro deficit, gross deformity / dislocation, or compartment-syndrome signs?

nodes.body: EMERGENT orthopaedics (± vascular / trauma). Open fracture: photograph, remove gross debris, saline-moist sterile dressing, IV antibiotics within 1 h (cefazolin 2 g; add gentamicin for gross contamination, penicillin for farm/soil), tetanus, splint in position of deformity, do NOT irrigate vigorously in the ED. Dislocation with deficit: reduce now. Hard vascular sign: vascular surgery + CT angiogram, do not wait.

Compartment syndrome — pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesia (pulselessness is late). Remove all circumferential dressing/cast, keep the limb at heart level (not elevated), analgesia, and get compartment pressures + emergent fasciotomy. ΔP (diastolic − compartment pressure) < 30 mmHg is diagnostic. Highest risk: tib-fib, forearm, high-energy, crush, reperfusion.

Closed reduction: adequate analgesia first (haematoma block, regional block, or procedural sedation — see the linked workflow). Recreate the mechanism, apply longitudinal traction, then reverse the deformity. Re-check and DOCUMENT neurovascular status before and after. Post-reduction film in the splint. Acceptable alignment varies by bone and age — if not achieved in 1–2 attempts, splint and refer for definitive management.

Buddy tape or aluminium U-splint in the position of function (MCP 70–90°, IP slight flexion). Check digital capillary refill and 2-point discrimination. Follow-up 1 week; early motion for stable non-displaced fractures.

ANY rotational deformity needs reduction — check by looking at nail-plate alignment and that all fingertips point to the scaphoid on flexion. Digital block, reduce, buddy-tape or gutter splint, post-reduction film. Refer hand/ortho if unstable, intra-articular > 1–2 mm step-off, or > 10° angulation in the fingers (more angulation tolerated at the 4th–5th MC neck).
Dorsal blocking splint with the PIP in ~20–30° flexion; early protected motion. Refer hand if > 30–40% of the articular surface is involved or the joint subluxates (may need surgery).

DIP extension splint (Stack or moulded) CONTINUOUSLY for 6–8 weeks, then night splinting 2–4 weeks — the DIP must not be allowed to flex at any point. Refer hand if there is a large bony fragment (> 30–50% articular) or volar subluxation of the distal phalanx.
Bennett (2-part) and Rolando (comminuted) fractures of the thumb-metacarpal base are intra-articular and unstable — thumb spica splint and refer hand surgery; most need percutaneous pinning or ORIF.

choices.label: Any with a 'fight bite' laceration over the MCP

nodes.body: 5th MC neck: up to ~40° apex-dorsal angulation is acceptable (little finger); reduce (Jahss manoeuvre) if more, or if there is rotational deformity or a pseudoclawing extensor lag. Ulnar gutter splint, MCP 70–90° flexion, IP extension, for 3–4 weeks. Always check for rotation.

Acceptable angulation decreases radially: ~10–20° for the 2nd–3rd, ~30–40° for the 4th–5th. Radial or ulnar gutter (or a hand-based splint), MCP 70–90°. Reduce and refer if angulation exceeds this, any rotation, > 5 mm shortening, or multiple MC fractures.

'Fight bite' — a laceration over the MCP from a tooth. Assume joint-space and extensor-tendon involvement. Do NOT close primarily. Explore in the OR / with hand surgery, IV amoxicillin-clavulanate (or ampicillin-sulbactam), tetanus, splint. High infection and septic-arthritis risk.

Volar (or sugar-tong if unstable) splint. Wrist ~20° extension, slight ulnar deviation, MCPs free. Check median (esp. — acute carpal tunnel), ulnar and radial nerve function, and finger flexion/extension. Ortho follow-up ~1 week; repeat film at 1–2 weeks to check for late displacement.

Reduce (haematoma block or sedation): traction, exaggerate the deformity, then translate the distal fragment volarly and correct radial shortening/tilt. Sugar-tong splint. Post-reduction film. Acceptable: radial length within ~2–3 mm, dorsal tilt ≤ ~5–10°, intra-articular step ≤ 2 mm — otherwise refer for fixation. Recheck the median nerve after reduction.

Snuffbox / scaphoid-tubercle tenderness with a normal X-ray = presumed scaphoid fracture. Thumb spica splint, ortho follow-up 10–14 days with repeat imaging (or MRI/CT earlier). Missed scaphoid fractures go on to non-union and avascular necrosis — immobilise and refer even when the film is clean.

Perilunate / lunate dislocation is frequently missed. Check the lateral wrist film for the 'spilled teacup' (lunate) and disrupted Gilula's arcs on the PA. Emergent hand-surgery reduction — high rate of median-nerve injury and long-term dysfunction if delayed.

choices.label: Both-bone forearm, or any displacement / angulation

nodes.body: Isolated non-displaced ulnar shaft (< 50% displacement, < 10° angulation): functional forearm brace or a well-moulded sugar-tong / long-arm splint, forearm neutral, elbow 90°. Check the radial, median and ulnar nerves and the radial pulse. Ortho follow-up 1 week.

Adult both-bone and displaced forearm shaft fractures are unstable — nearly all need ORIF. Provisional closed reduction for gross deformity/neurovascular compromise, long-arm splint at 90° with the forearm in neutral rotation, and urgent ortho referral. In children these are often managed closed with reduction + casting.

Monteggia — proximal ulna fracture WITH radial-head dislocation. Always draw a radiocapitellar line on every elbow/forearm film: it should bisect the capitellum in every view. Missed radial-head dislocation is a classic and disabling error. Long-arm splint and urgent ortho — adults need ORIF.

Galeazzi — distal-third radius fracture WITH distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) disruption. Look for widened DRUJ, radial shortening, ulnar styloid fracture, or a prominent ulnar head. 'Fracture of necessity' in adults — ORIF. Long-arm splint, forearm supinated, urgent ortho.

choices.label: Effusion / fat pad, no visible fracture

nodes.body: Non-displaced / minimally-displaced (Mason I) radial-head fracture: sling or a long-arm posterior splint at 90° for comfort, then EARLY range of motion within a few days to prevent stiffness. Aspiration of the haematoma + local anaesthetic can improve early motion. Ortho follow-up 1 week. Displaced or mechanical block → ortho.

Posterior long-arm splint at 45–90° flexion. Check ulnar nerve function and the integrity of active elbow extension (a displaced fracture disrupts the triceps mechanism → needs fixation). Displacement > 2 mm or extensor lag → ortho for tension-band or plate fixation.

Paediatric supracondylar humerus — assess and document the anterior interosseous nerve (OK sign), radial nerve, ulnar nerve, and the radial pulse / hand perfusion. Gartland I (non-displaced): long-arm posterior splint at 60–90°, ortho follow-up. Gartland II–III, any pulseless / poorly perfused hand, or a nerve deficit: EMERGENT ortho for closed reduction and pinning. A pulseless but well-perfused (pink) hand still goes urgently to theatre.

Reduce a posterior elbow dislocation promptly (procedural sedation): traction–countertraction with the elbow slightly flexed, correct medial/lateral translation, then flex. Confirm a concentric reduction on film and re-examine the ulnar and median nerves and the brachial artery. Splint at 90° in a posterior long-arm splint; early protected motion by ~1 week to avoid stiffness. Recurrent instability, an associated fracture, or a non-concentric reduction → ortho.

A posterior fat-pad sign (or a large anterior 'sail' sign) with no visible fracture means an occult intra-articular fracture — radial head in adults, supracondylar in children. Treat as a non-displaced fracture: long-arm posterior splint / sling, ortho follow-up 7–10 days with repeat films.

Midshaft: coaptation (U-slab) splint or a sugar-tong for the arm, then transition to a functional (Sarmiento) brace at ~1 week. Acceptable: < 20° anterior angulation, < 30° varus/valgus, < 3 cm shortening — most heal well non-operatively. Arm adducted, elbow 90°. Ortho follow-up 1 week.

Most (1-part / minimally displaced Neer) are treated with a sling and early pendulum exercises at 7–14 days. Check axillary-nerve sensation over the deltoid. Refer ortho for displacement > 1 cm or angulation > 45°, greater-tuberosity displacement > 5 mm, fracture-dislocation, or a head-split.

Radial-nerve palsy (wrist drop, loss of finger/thumb extension, dorsal first-web-space sensory loss) complicates ~10–18% of midshaft fractures — most are neurapraxia and recover over 3–4 months. A NEW deficit appearing after reduction/manipulation, or an open fracture, is an indication for surgical exploration. Splint, cock-up wrist splint for the drop, and ortho referral.

Buddy tape to the adjacent toe, hard-soled shoe, neutral. Check capillary refill. Reduce an angulated or rotated fracture (digital block). Great-toe fractures and any intra-articular or displaced fracture → podiatry/ortho follow-up. Open (often from a nailbed laceration) → antibiotics + tetanus.

Tuberosity avulsion (zone 1): good blood supply, heals well. Hard-soled shoe or walking boot, weight-bear as tolerated, 4–6 weeks. Follow-up podiatry/ortho. Only large intra-articular (> 30%) or widely displaced fragments need referral for possible fixation.

True Jones fracture (zone 2, metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction): watershed blood supply → high non-union rate. Non-weight-bearing in a short-leg cast / boot for 6–8 weeks, ortho follow-up. Many active patients (and any zone-3 proximal-diaphyseal stress fracture) are offered early intramedullary screw fixation.

Isolated 2nd–4th MT shaft, minimally displaced: walking boot / hard-soled shoe, weight-bear as tolerated, 4–6 weeks. Refer for > 3–4 mm translation or > 10° dorsoplantar angulation (alters weight distribution), or multiple adjacent MT fractures.

Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury — plantar-medial ecchymosis, midfoot swelling, pain on midfoot pronation/abduction, inability to bear weight. Look for a fleck sign (avulsion between 1st and 2nd MT bases) and > 2 mm diastasis on a weight-bearing AP; get weight-bearing or CT imaging if the initial films are normal but suspicion is high. Non-weight-bearing splint and urgent ortho — a missed Lisfranc is a limb with chronic pain and arthritis.

choices.label: Bimalleolar / trimalleolar, or talar shift on mortise view

nodes.body: Isolated non-displaced lateral (Weber A / low B) malleolus with a congruent mortise and no medial tenderness: walking boot or a well-moulded posterior + stirrup splint, ankle at 90° neutral, weight-bear as tolerated, ortho follow-up ~1 week. Check dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and sensation.

Bimalleolar, trimalleolar, any talar shift / widened medial clear space, or a Weber C (syndesmotic) pattern = unstable → ORIF. Non-weight-bearing posterior + stirrup splint at 90°, elevate, ortho referral (within days). Watch the skin over a tented medial malleolus.

Reduce a deformed / dislocated ankle BEFORE imaging if the skin is tented or the foot is dusky (do not wait for X-ray). Procedural sedation, traction on the heel and foot with counter-traction on the calf, recreate then reverse the deformity. Splint at 90°, re-check pulses and skin, then image. Emergent ortho.

choices.label: Open, displaced, or any compartment concern

nodes.body: Long-leg posterior splint (± AP slabs), knee 5–15° flexion, ankle 90°. Generous padding, NO circumferential cast acutely. Check the deep peroneal nerve (first web-space sensation, foot/toe dorsiflexion) and distal pulses, and do a baseline compartment exam. Admit or urgent ortho — many tibial shaft fractures need an IM nail, and this is the highest-risk site for compartment syndrome (serial exams).

Non-displaced (< 2–3 mm step, < 3 mm fragment separation) with an intact extensor mechanism: knee immobiliser in extension, weight-bear as tolerated with crutches, ortho follow-up ~1 week, early quad sets. Check for an open injury (the patella is subcutaneous).

Inability to perform a straight-leg raise or a palpable defect = extensor-mechanism disruption (displaced patella fracture, or patellar/quadriceps tendon rupture) → operative repair. Knee immobiliser in extension, non-weight-bearing, ortho referral within days.

Tibial plateau fracture: knee immobiliser or long-leg splint, NON-weight-bearing, elevate. High-energy patterns — do a careful compartment exam and check the popliteal vessels and peroneal nerve. Most need CT for surgical planning; displaced / depressed (> 2–3 mm articular step, or condylar widening) → ORIF. Suspect an occult fracture with a lipohaemarthrosis on X-ray.

Knee dislocation is a vascular emergency even when it has spontaneously reduced. Popliteal artery injury in ~20–30%. Reduce immediately if still dislocated, then: ABIs on BOTH legs (< 0.9 → CT angiogram / vascular surgery), serial pulse and compartment checks, immobilise at 20° flexion, admit. A normal pulse does NOT exclude an intimal injury.

Femoral SHAFT fracture: a traction splint (Hare / Sager / CT-6) is the prehospital and ED bridge for a mid-shaft fracture with no associated pelvic, knee, or open injury — it controls bleeding (1–1.5 L into the thigh) and pain. Analgesia, check femoral and distal pulses and the sciatic/peroneal nerve, screen for the high-energy associated injuries (pelvis, hip, ipsilateral femoral neck — a classic miss). Femoral NECK / intertrochanteric fracture (older patient, shortened + externally rotated leg): NO traction splint — a pillow/blanket for comfort, analgesia (consider a fascia-iliaca block), admit for fixation, and check for the medical cause of the fall.

choices.label: Buckle / torus (one cortex buckled, e.g. distal radius)
Greenstick (one cortex broken, the other bent)
Toddler's fracture (spiral distal tibia, will not weight-bear)
Any red flag for non-accidental trauma

nodes.body: Torus / buckle fracture — inherently stable. A removable wrist/volar splint (or a soft brace) for 3–4 weeks, no reduction, and no routine repeat X-ray or ortho visit needed for a classic distal-radius buckle — primary-care or virtual follow-up is sufficient. Return if pain persists past 4 weeks.

Greenstick: if angulation exceeds the age-acceptable limit (more remodelling potential the younger the child and the closer to the physis, in the plane of joint motion), reduce — often by completing the fracture — then a well-moulded long-arm cast/splint. Minimal angulation: immobilise and refer. Repeat film at 1 week for loss of position.

Plastic (bowing) deformation — the bone is bent without a discrete fracture line, commonly the ulna or fibula alongside a fracture of the paired bone. Significant bowing (> ~20°, or a cosmetic/functional deformity, or blocking forearm rotation) needs reduction under sedation; otherwise immobilise and refer. It does not remodel as reliably as a true fracture.

Salter-Harris — 'SALTR': I Slipped (through physis; X-ray may be normal — tender physis = treat as SH-I), II Above (into metaphysis; commonest), III Lower (into epiphysis/joint), IV Through (metaphysis + physis + epiphysis), V cRush (axial compression; worst prognosis, often diagnosed late). Splint I–II and refer; III–V are intra-articular or high-risk for growth arrest → prompt ortho, often ORIF. Always document neurovascular status and counsel families about the growth-disturbance risk.

Toddler's fracture — non-displaced spiral fracture of the distal tibia in a 9-month to 3-year-old who suddenly will not bear weight; the initial X-ray is often normal (repeat at 1–2 weeks shows periosteal reaction). Long-leg or a controlled-ankle walking boot for 3–4 weeks. If the history is inconsistent or there are other injuries, evaluate for non-accidental trauma.

Consider non-accidental trauma in any child with: a fracture in a non-ambulatory infant, a history inconsistent with the injury or the developmental stage, delayed presentation, multiple fractures of different ages, or classic patterns (classic metaphyseal 'corner/bucket-handle' lesions, posterior rib fractures, scapular/sternal/spinous-process fractures). Follow local safeguarding pathways and get a skeletal survey.

checklist: Neurovascular status assessed and DOCUMENTED before any manipulation
Screened for the emergent patterns (open, vascular hard sign, compartment syndrome, dislocation, progressive deficit)
Adequate analgesia / haematoma block / procedural sedation before any reduction attempt
Splint applied with generous padding — no acute circumferential casting
Neurovascular status re-checked and re-DOCUMENTED after splinting / reduction
Post-reduction film obtained in the splint where a reduction was performed
Paediatric: growth-plate involvement identified; non-accidental trauma considered where the history does not fit
Discharge: elevation, return precautions (increasing pain, numbness, colour change, tight cast), ortho follow-up timeframe given

buildNote: v2 — 2-level tree using the existing procedure.nodes structure (interactive walker already renders it on web + iOS). `gate-emergent`, `compartment`, and `emergent` are shared nodes referenced from multiple branches. Reduction technique is generic (`reduce-generic`) plus bone-specific acceptable-alignment thresholds in each leaf. Nerve Block and POCUS guides remain reference-style menus — converting them to node trees is a separate, lower-value pass.
